concepts.title: Marr's Vision Philosophy and Influences
concepts.one_liner: David Marr's influential philosophy of vision was shaped by advances in computer vision, cognitive psychology, and neurophysiology, emphasizing independent modules of perception and neural activity.
concepts.content: David Marr's influential book Vision was published posthumously in 1982. Marr's philosophy was influenced by advances in computer vision, and studies in cognitive psychology and neurophysiology. Studies in psychology at the time suggested that visual information was processed by independent modules of perception, each one devoted to a specific task (stereo vision, motion perception, color processing), and that visual images were analyzed by independent spatial-frequency-tuned channels. Progress in neurophysiological experiments using single cell recordings showed a strong connection between perception and neural activity. In the 1970s, computer vision was already a well-established field. Some of the advances that inspired Marr's philosophy were the work by David L. Waltz on the interpretation of block worlds, Edwin H. Land and John J. McCann's Retinex theory about color perception, and Berthold Horn's theory of shape from shading, among many other works.
concepts.motivation_md: Marr sought to provide a rigorous framework for understanding vision by integrating findings from psychology, neuroscience, and computer science, moving beyond simple descriptions of neural activity to a systematic theory of how biological and artificial systems process visual information.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is processed by independent modules devoted to specific tasks like stereo vision and color processing.

concepts.title: Vision as an Information-Processing Task
concepts.one_liner: David Marr postulated that vision should be understood as an information-processing task, separating the analysis of the task from the mechanism used to solve it.
concepts.content: David Marr, together with Tomaso Poggio and others, postulated that it was important to separate the analysis of the task being solved from the particular mechanism used to solve it. Marr said that the vision problem should be understood at different levels, and that what was missing in previous theories of vision was to understand vision as an information-processing task.
concepts.motivation_md: To solve complex visual problems, it is necessary to define the abstract goal of the computation independently of whether it is being performed by a brain or a computer.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is fundamentally an information-processing task.

concepts.title: Marr's Computational Theory Level
concepts.one_liner: The computational theory level defines what task is being performed and why, specifying the mapping between input and output without detailing the algorithm.
concepts.content: The computational theory level of description should answer the following questions: what is the task to be performed and why should it be carried out? In the case of vision, the task is to derive properties of the world from images. This level of description should specify what the mapping is between the input and output, and why this mapping is appropriate for the task that the device needs to solve. This level does not specify how that mapping should be constructed or which algorithm will implement it.
concepts.motivation_md: This level provides the necessary abstract foundation for understanding a system's purpose before worrying about implementation details.

concepts.title: Marr's Representation Level
concepts.one_liner: The representation level defines the system used to make explicit certain types of information in a signal, which strongly influences the algorithm's performance.
concepts.content: The representation level defines which representation will be used for the input and output. The representation is a system of making explicit certain types of information present on a signal. For instance, an image could be represented by the sequence of values that encode the color of each pixel, but it could be also represented using a Fourier decomposition. The choice of representation will make explicit certain types of information while hiding other information, which will become harder to access. The algorithm used to implement the mapping between input and output will be strongly dependent on the representation used. The importance of the choice of representation is very present in today's computer vision community. Examples such as using position encoding to represent location illustrate the dramatic effect that the choice of representation and algorithm can have in the final system performance.
concepts.motivation_md: The choice of representation determines which information is easily accessible to an algorithm, directly impacting the efficiency and success of the visual task.

concepts.title: Marr's Hardware Level
concepts.one_liner: The hardware level describes the physical implementation of the representation and algorithm in a device.
concepts.content:
The hardware level is where the representation and algorithm are implemented in a physical device. Marr noted that when trying to explain visual phenomena, one needs to find what is the right level to use to describe it. For instance, the trichromatic color theory of human perception is explained by the hardware level (i.e., by the three color receptors in our retina) while the bistable nature of the Necker cube is likely to be related to the 3D representation. The illusions shown in @fig-measuringScene are also likely due to the representation and algorithm used and they are rather independent on the particular hardware implementation. Marr considered that Gibson was asking the right questions, getting very close to a computational theory of vision, but that he had a naive view on how difficult it would be to solve them.

concepts.title: Marr's Sequence of Representations
concepts.one_liner: Marr proposed that vision is implemented as a sequence of representations, transforming raw pixel intensities into explicit 3D model representations.
concepts.content:
In David Marr's approach, vision was implemented as a sequence of representations, starting from the image represented as a sequence of pixel intensities, and then transforming each representation into another one that extracts more explicit information about the geometry and objects present in the world. The sequence of representations proposed by Marr was the following:

- Image: The collection of pixel intensities.

- Primal sketch: Represents changes in the image (edges, junctions, zero-crossings) and their spatial organization.

- 2.5D sketch: Contains an estimation of the distance between the observer and the visible surfaces in the world at each pixel, also called a **depth map**. It also contains information about depth discontinuities and surface orientations.

- 3D model representation: Objects are represented as 3D shapes together with their spatial organization.

There is a strong parallelism between the sequence of representations proposed by Marr and the particular algorithm discussed when building a simple visual system. @fig-sketch shows the image of a cube, and its 2.5D sketch as proposed by Marr. The arrows (**gauge-figures**) represent surface orientation. The dashed lines are surface orientation discontinuities and the black lines are occlusion boundaries. The pixel intensities represent distance between the observer and the visible surfaces of the cube. Depth is represented by gray levels, where intensity increases with depth.

![Image of a cube, and its 2.5D sketch. Figure inspired from figure 4-2 from @Marr82.](figures/taxonomy/sketch.png){#fig-sketch width="90%"}
concepts.motivation_md: Breaking vision into a sequence of stages allows for the incremental extraction of complex geometric and object-level information from simple light intensity data.

concepts.title: The ImageNet Moment
concepts.one_liner: The ImageNet Moment refers to the 2012 watershed event where deep learning began to dominate computer vision research.
concepts.content: The "ImageNet Moment" refers to the event where AlexNet's dramatic performance was first demonstrated at the 2012 ImageNet competition. This event was a watershed for learning-based vision and for neural networks. In the few years after 2012, learning became the key ingredient in almost all research on computer vision. As of the 2020s, it is hard to find any computer vision system that does not use deep learning somewhere in its pipeline.

concepts.title: The Nature of Learning-Based Vision
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision uses automated learners to find the mapping between input and output, rather than relying on human-designed algorithms.
concepts.content: The study of vision consists of the structure of the input, the structure of the output, and the mapping between the two. Learning-based vision does not fundamentally change any of these: the input and target output are the same as before, and the mapping is remarkably similar as in other approaches. The big difference with learning-based vision is how you *find* the mapping. In this sense, learners are just like a new kind of vision scientist: they play the same role as the humans who, in previous eras, sat down and thought deeply to determine the way vision works. Very often machine learners come up with similar vision algorithms as were previously designed by humans, but machine learners are also more powerful than human designers, and machine learned algorithms have now far exceeded those designed by humans in terms of raw performance.
concepts.motivation_md: Learning-based vision automates the discovery of complex visual mappings that are too difficult for humans to design manually.

concepts.title: Ambient Light
concepts.one_liner: Ambient light is the complex structure of light rays, including reflections and shadows, that fills an environment.
concepts.content: Ambient light is a term coined by James J. Gibson to describe the complex structure of light in an environment, characterized by multiple reflections, shadows, and specular surfaces. concepts.title: Plenoptic Function
concepts.one_liner: The plenoptic function describes the light intensity of every ray in space across direction, wavelength, and time.
concepts.content:
The pattern of light filling the space can be described by the function: $$P (\theta, \Phi, \lambda, t, X, Y, Z)$$ where $P$ is the light intensity of a ray passing by the world location $(X,Y,Z)$ in the direction given by the angle $(\theta, \Phi)$, and with wavelength $\lambda$ at an instant in time $t$. This function, called the **plenoptic function** by Edward H. Adelson and James R. Bergen, contains all the information needed to describe the complete pattern of light rays that fills the space.

Plenoptic function: Edward H. Adelson was going to call it the *holoscopic function*, but a well-known holographer told him that he would punch him in the nose if he called it that.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a complete mathematical representation of all visual information available in a scene.
concepts.recap_md:
- The plenoptic function $P (\theta, \Phi, \lambda, t, X, Y, Z)$ captures all light rays in a space.
 - It accounts for position, direction, wavelength, and time.

concepts.title: Role of Occlusion in Vision
concepts.one_liner: Occlusion occurs when surfaces are hidden from view, presenting a significant challenge for visual interpretation.
concepts.content: For a given observer, most of the light rays are occluded. Occlusion is a primary example of the difficulty of vision; properly interpreting an image often requires understanding which parts are hidden. For instance, we understand a person is not floating if their legs are occluded behind a table. Occlusions are extremely common, as there are typically more occluded surfaces than visible ones for any observer.
concepts.motivation_md: Occlusion is a fundamental constraint of 3D scenes that forces the visual system to make inferences about hidden information.
concepts.recap_md:

 - Interpreting occlusions is essential for understanding spatial relationships and object depth.

concepts.title: Visual Awareness

concepts.title: Center-Surround Receptive Field Organization
concepts.one_liner: Ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization that enables contrast enhancement.
concepts.content: Ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization. There are two primary types: on-center cells, which activate when light hits the middle of the receptive field and deactivate when light hits the surrounding ring, and off-center cells, which exhibit the opposite behavior. This organization reveals that the retina performs contrast enhancing operations. In an ON-center receptive field, illumination of the inner part increases the firing rate, while stimulation of the outer part inhibits the response.
concepts.motivation_md: This organization allows the retina to perform contrast enhancement and edge detection before signals reach the brain, serving as an efficient way to process visual information.

concepts.title: On-center and Off-center Ganglion Cells
concepts.one_liner: On-center and off-center cells are ganglion cells that respond antagonistically to light in the center versus the surround of their receptive fields.

Off-center cells exhibit the opposite behavior, being inhibited by light in the center and excited by light in the surround.

concepts.title: Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
concepts.one_liner: The lateral geniculate nucleus is a six-layered relay structure that transmits monocular visual information from the retina to the cortex.
concepts.content: The axons of ganglion cells from both eyes project to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a structure composed of six layers of neurons that outputs to the visual cortex. The LGN receives inputs from both eyes, but the signals are not mixed and the neurons remain monocular. LGN neurons have concentric center-surround receptive fields. While its role is not completely understood, it may be involved in temporal decorrelation, attention modulation, and saccadic suppression. Interestingly, only 5 percent of the input connections come from the retina, while 95 percent are feedback connections from the primary visual cortex and other areas.
concepts.motivation_md: The LGN acts as a sophisticated relay station that filters and modulates visual information from the retina before it reaches the cortex, influenced heavily by top-down feedback.

concepts.title: Learning-Based vs. Model-Based Perception
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision focuses on data and flexible architectures rather than predefined models of how perception works.
concepts.content: While many previous perspectives on perception began with models about how perception might work, learning-based approaches take a different path. They rely on flexible architectures that incorporate as few hypotheses about perception as possible, and instead focus on data to learn to build the right model for perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional model-based approaches often rely on rigid assumptions that may not capture the complexity of the real world; learning-based methods allow the data to define the model.

- Learning-based approaches minimize initial hypotheses about perception.
- They prioritize data-driven model building over predefined theoretical models.

concepts.title: Three Approaches to Programming Vision Algorithms
concepts.one_liner: Vision algorithms can be programmed directly, derived from world models, or learned from data by fitting functions to examples.
concepts.content: Learning derives vision algorithms by fitting functions to data. One way to think about it is that our goal is to "program" a vision algorithm and there are a few ways to do so (@fig-taxonomy-programming_vs_learning). One way is to write the algorithm directly in Python code: first we will compare the intensity of this pixel and that pixel, then we will threshold about some such value, and so on. Another approach is to derive the algorithm as the rational thing to do given some underlying model of the world; for example, because overlapping objects generically produce contrast edges in the image, the optimal way to detect boundaries between objects is to look for a particular kind of contrast. The third approach—the learning approach—is to program algorithms via data: first collect a bunch of examples of inputs and the correct output, then fit a function that replicates these exemplar mappings from input to output. ![Two ways of programming an algorithm. Left: traditional way, Right: the machine learning way. You will learn about the machine learning "compiler", called Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), in .](figures/taxonomy/programming_vs_learning.png){#fig-taxonomy-programming_vs_learning width="100%"}
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these three approaches helps clarify the evolution from manual feature engineering and physical modeling to modern data-driven machine learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Direct programming involves manual coding of pixel-level logic.
- Model-based derivation uses rational principles of the physical world.
- The learning approach fits functions to input-output data pairs.

concepts.title: Affordance
concepts.one_liner: An affordance is a property of an object or environment that provides an opportunity for action to an observer.
concepts.content: Introduced by Gibson in 1966, an affordance refers to the action possibilities provided by the environment. For example, a path affords locomotion, an obstacle affords collision, and a stairway affords both descent and ascent. The affordance of an object is generally a direct consequence of its properties: a hollow object can contain substances, a detached object affords carrying, and an object with a sharp edge affords cutting. Animate objects are controlled by internal forces and afford social interaction.
concepts.motivation_md: It explains how perception is directly linked to action, allowing organisms to identify functional opportunities in their environment immediately.

concepts.title: Direct Perception
concepts.one_liner: Direct perception is the process of picking up information directly from the ambient optic array without the need for additional mental processing.
concepts.content: Gibson's theory of visual perception postulates that the ambient optic array is very rich and contains all the information needed to perceive the environment. Direct perception is the process of information pickup directly from the ambient array. This is in contrast with other theories of visual perception that assume that the input stimuli is very impoverished and that perception is indirect as it has to be complemented by additional processes. When building a perceptual system, a richer input might allow for a simpler solution to the perception problem.
concepts.motivation_md: It simplifies the problem of perception by suggesting that the environment itself provides all necessary information, reducing the need for complex internal computations.

concepts.one_liner: Santiago Ramón y Cajal proved that the brain is composed of networks of individual, interconnected cells rather than a continuous mass.
concepts.content:
In 1890, Santiago Ramón y Cajal used Golgi's stain to isolate individual neurons and proved that the brain is composed of networks of interconnected cells, as shown in his work on the anatomy of the retina. This was the first time that networks were observed. Ramón y Cajal then mapped most of the brain, and his drawings remain a reference. Both Santiago Ramón y Cajal and Camillo Golgi received the Nobel Prize in 1906.

concepts.title: Functional Anatomy of the Retina
concepts.one_liner: The retina is a complex neural circuit that transforms light into electrical impulses and processes them through multiple layers of specialized neurons.
concepts.content:
The retina is an amazing piece of the brain that transforms light into impulses. Light is first transformed into electric signals by the photoreceptors (rods and cones) and is then processed by a few layers formed by several types of neurons, including amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells. Finally, ganglion cells transmit the output of the retina through the optic nerve to the rest of the brain. The studies of Ramón y Cajal revealed the circuitry of many parts of the brain but told us little about their functional behavior or how the circuits were processing information.

concepts.title: Goal of Vision: Interpretation vs. Measurement
concepts.one_liner: The goal of vision is to provide an interpretation of the world in terms of "meaningful" surfaces, objects, and materials to extract relevant elements.
concepts.content: If the goal of vision were simply to measure the light intensity coming from a particular direction of space like a photometer, then things would be easy. However, the goal of vision is to provide an interpretation of the world in terms of "meaningful" surfaces, objects, and materials to extract all the different elements that compose the scene. This problem is hard because most information is lost, requiring the visual system to make assumptions about the structure of the world to recover information from a small sample of the plenoptic function. It is also difficult because our understanding of what is relevant for the observer is incomplete.
concepts.motivation_md: Vision exists to help observers interact with their environment by identifying objects and surfaces, which is much more complex than simple light measurement.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision interprets the world as meaningful objects and materials rather than just measuring light intensity. - The visual system uses assumptions to recover lost information from the environment.

concepts.title: Recovery of Scene Properties
concepts.one_liner: The human visual system extracts scene properties relevant for the observer by automatically interpreting images as pictures of real three-dimensional scenes.

concepts.title: Turning Tables Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The turning tables illusion demonstrates how the visual system's automatic 3D interpretation makes two identical 2D shapes appear to have different lengths.
concepts.content: The "turning tables illusion" by Roger Shepard demonstrates that we cannot shut down the automatic mechanisms that interpret images as pictures of real three-dimensional (3D) scenes. In this illusion, both table tops have the same shape and size but one is rotated with respect to the other. The visual system insists in interpreting these objects as 3D objects, giving the impression that the left table is longer than the table on the right. This perception cannot be shut down even if we know exactly how this image has been generated.

concepts.title: Checkershadow Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The checkershadow illusion shows how the visual system infers true surface reflectance by removing the effects of shadows from its perception.
concepts.content: The "checkershadow illusion" by Adelson illustrates that the visual system interprets images as pictures of real three-dimensional (3D) scenes rather than just light patterns. In this figure, the squares marked with A and B have the exact same intensity values. However, the visual system tries to measure the surface reflectance of the squares, removing the effect of the shadow to infer the true gray value of each square. As a result, the square in the shadow is perceived as being lighter than the square outside the shadow region, even though both have the same gray levels.

concepts.one_liner: Computer vision tasks range from motion estimation and object recognition to building 3D models and understanding animal behavior.
concepts.content: The goal of vision is to provide the observer with information relevant to understanding the outside world and to enable tasks such as navigating, interacting with agents, and finding food. Tasks within computer vision include detecting changes in the environment, motion estimation, object recognition and localization, and recognizing materials. Other tasks include reading text, building 3D models, finding free space to move, finding other people, deciding if food is in a good state, and understanding the behavior of animals. Some tasks seem to require significant external knowledge, while others may be solvable from the images alone.

concepts.title: Gibson's Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
concepts.one_liner: Gibson's ecological approach suggests that vision should be studied in the context of the observer's body and their natural environment.
concepts.content: James J. Gibson postulated that understanding vision requires an ecological approach to visual perception, studying the eye in the context of the body and the world it lives in. While simple visual stimuli in controlled labs allow for reproducible findings, they are too limiting to unravel the true nature of the visual system. Gibson argued that the environment should be studied by means of ecological properties, such as medium (air or water), substances (rocks, metal, wood), and surfaces, together with the notions of change and persistence. These concepts are considered more relevant to perception than the notions of space, matter, and time found in classical physics.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach shifted the focus of perception research from abstract physics to the functional relationship between an organism and its environment.
